paragraphs: On the fifth day after the fires of Chang’an, an encampment said to house thirty thousand men rose on the north bank of the Wei River.

Thirty thousand was the sum reported by the commanders of the several forces. At close range, the camps held armored soldiers newly arrived with Fu Luo from Beidi, imperial household troops hastily added to the army, and village militiamen swept up on the march. Hundreds of tents ran together, but each group of men and horses answered to its own standard. At midnight one unit wandered into another’s horse lines and was driven out by arrows. By daylight, some had replaced the white strips on their banners with black, claiming to mourn the clansmen who had died in Chang’an’s fires.

The Wei was rising. Rain had fallen upstream the previous night, and yellow, turbid water submerged the fine grass along the banks. Swift eddies formed around the bridge piers. South of the bridge the new army had set its barriers in a single line. It carried fewer banners, but its ranks were orderly. Smoke from Chang’an drifted with the wind; at the bridgehead there were moments when the smell of wet charcoal reached the men.

Fu Luo sat in his tent on the northern bank with a confidential letter freshly delivered. The rebel captain Fu Jian was dead. Nearly all the advance cavalry that had entered the city had been lost; Zhangcheng Gate had been shut again. Someone in the palace claimed the Heavenly King had kept watch from a tower all night without sleep. Fu Luo crumpled the letter and smoothed it out, reading again and again the line recording Fu Jian’s death. The two of them had agreed that if the advance guard reached the city first, it would harm no civilians, ask the Heavenly King to come out amid the confusion, and never force its way into the palace. Now the man who knew the agreement was dead, and there was no one left to explain what it had meant.
His chief secretary said, “If we storm Chang’an, every garrison in the empire will believe that Your Highness truly has rebelled.”
Fu Luo watched the gray-yellow water beyond the bridge. “And if I do not fight, what do you call this army I have brought here?”

The secretary hesitated. “We could send an envoy first. Demand that Murong Chui and Quan Yi be surrendered, that the mixed-army system be suspended, and that the imperial household regain its former commands. Then Your Highness could lay aside your armor and plead guilty.”

The conditions sounded simple enough. Everyone knew Fu Jian could scarcely accept them. Even so, Fu Luo agreed to send a messenger. He waited in armor until noon, one hand resting on the old sword at the corner of the table. Its grip had been polished bright by years of use and looked just as it had when he first marched to Beidi.

In Chengming Hall the envoy crawled forward and presented the three demands. Quan Yi read them and asked, “If the Duke of Beihai merely wishes to air his grievances at court, why has he brought armed men into the approaches to the capital?” The messenger answered that the people of Beidi had received a secret edict to protect the sovereign. Someone in the hall lost his temper. Fu Jian instead ordered the document put away and asked, “If I agree, will he first disband his army?”
The envoy said nothing.
There was nowhere left for the negotiations to go. Fu Jian descended the steps of the dais. “Bring my horse. I am going to Wei Bridge.”
The Crown Prince immediately stepped in front of him. “Father, the north bank is full of soldiers. You cannot simply go there.”
“If I refuse to show myself, Fu Luo will have a thousand things to say about why.”

Murong Chui asked leave to send cavalry ahead and seize the ford. Fu Jian shook his head. He permitted only three thousand soldiers of the mixed army to accompany him. The rest would hold Chang’an’s gates and were forbidden to move without orders. Yao Chang asked to ride with him but was left to guard the city. Before departing, Fu Jian exchanged his ceremonial robes for an old suit of armor he had worn many years earlier. Tiny cracks ran along the edges of its plates. The palace servants urged him to wear new armor, but he refused.

The Heavenly King rode out of the northern gate without drums, music, or a long ceremonial escort. A single Qin banner went before him. Fu Hong rode close beside his father. As Murong Chui passed through the gate, he looked back once. The freshly mended wooden stakes along Chang’an’s walls had not yet been painted, and burned roofs still showed their bare rafters. Since the empty seat at the spring banquet, events had moved toward this meeting one step at a time.

On the north side of the bridge, Fu Luo rode out to meet him with twenty horsemen. He wore no helmet. The old scar above his right eyebrow stood out white against his skin. Fu Jian dismounted on the southern bank and walked onto the wet planks. Less than ten paces of empty bridge lay between the two men, with the sound of the river rising beneath it.
“Did you order men to set Chang’an on fire?” Fu Jian asked first.
Something leaped in Fu Luo’s eyes. “I gave no such order.”
“And Chang Xuan?”
“I did not order his murder either.”
“Yet you said cavalry from Dai killed him.”
Fu Luo was silent for a moment. “At that time I was still trying to save Beidi.”

Fu Jian studied him for a long time. When they were young, Fu Luo had once endured bitter cold at his side in an army camp. They had slept wrapped in the same sheepskin. Fu Luo, too young to know fear, had watched the entrance of his elder brother’s tent until, overcome by sleep, his head kept nodding against his sword hilt. The face before Fu Jian was the same face, but the years of wind and frost upon it spoke of grievances that had accumulated beyond counting.
“Here I am,” Fu Jian said. “You claim I am being held hostage. Where are the men holding me?”
Fu Luo’s gaze traveled past him toward Murong Chui.
“Him.”
“I ordered him to come.”
“Your Majesty will not even let the imperial clan keep its old retainers, yet you allow a man of fallen Yan to command thirty thousand soldiers of the new army.”
Murong Chui did not move behind Fu Jian. “He earned his merit with blood in Hexi and northern Dai,” the Heavenly King replied. “You have rendered service in Beidi too. What is the difference?”
Fu Luo’s lips twitched. “My service has to be checked by clerks against their registers. His can win him the troops of the whole realm.”
“He receives soldiers by appointment from the military offices and his supplies from the court. If he is replaced, he cannot carry the men away with him. The same rules apply to you.”

“Those veterans of mine have followed me for twenty years. I know which house has lost its husband, whose bones were shattered, better than any clerk in the Secretariat. Chang Xuan came into camp waving a register, telling me there were too many men here, too few there. He found a lame soldier and didn’t even know the man’s father had once taken an arrow meant for me!”
His words came faster, his voice roughening. “If Your Majesty scatters them, who is to repay the debt of that arrow?”

Fu Jian waited before answering. “Who should repay it, I cannot tell you. But this debt you speak of has become one that the living can never pay in full. A dead man’s son must draw his sword for you before he can draw his grain. A man who will not mount his horse is treated as though he owes you a debt.”
“Because the court has never truly cared for them!”
“If the court has failed them, make the court do better. Do not leave generations of them dependent on one general.”

Fu Luo clenched his teeth. He thrust a finger toward the soldiers ranked south of the bridge—Xianbei, Qiang, Han, and Di. “Do you believe these men will one day defend a realm ruled by the Fu clan? The men of Yan lost Yan and could serve Qin. If Qin falls, where will the Di have left to go?”

Fu Jian looked toward the formation. The soldiers' expressions differed. Some understood the whole exchange; others had caught only the word “Di” and tightened their grip on their spears. He turned back. “I fear that the Di will have nowhere to go, just as you do. But we cannot make our road by trampling other people beneath our feet. If Qin falls and every people comes to collect an old debt, how many can the private guards of the Fu clan protect?”
Fu Luo laughed coldly. “Then let Your Majesty give the Fu clan away to the whole world.”

There was little more to be said that would not tear open an older wound. Fu Jian mastered his rising anger. “Surrender the military registers. Return the detained messengers. Come back to the capital with me. The court will investigate Chang Xuan’s death point by point. Neither your merits nor your crimes will be written for you by someone else.”
Once his soldiers were gone, Fu Luo asked, who would listen to him?
“I am listening now.”

“Now Your Majesty has three thousand soldiers at your back!” Fu Luo’s voice suddenly rose. “I have thirty thousand behind me! If I come tomorrow with no more than a single carriage, will Your Majesty ride out personally to receive me then?”

Fu Jian’s hand rested motionless upon the clasp of his old armor. Fu Luo did not wait for his reply. He stepped back and put on his helmet. His officers saw the gesture and tightened their reins. From the north bank came the answering cry of war horns.
“Duke of Beihai!” Fu Jian called one final time.
Fu Luo looked at him but gave no answer.

Fu Jian turned and walked back across the bridge. Murong Chui met him, asking permission to take two thousand horsemen upstream and sweep around the enemy’s rear. Fu Jian refused. “Today I will not allow your Xianbei cavalry to slaughter Beidi soldiers from behind. Hold the bridge first. If they truly force the crossing, strike their flank.” Murong frowned, but at last bowed in obedience. He sent only five hundred riders to hold the shoals and kept the remainder in support.

The Crown Prince ordered the standard-bearer to move the Heavenly King’s flag behind the shield line. Fu Jian heard him. “The banner belongs with the central command. It must not be moved about.” Fu Hong looked toward the bridgehead. The defenders there had come off duty amid the fires only the night before. Their eyes were hollow with exhaustion and their shields still carried black scorch marks.
“Father,” he said, “if they cannot see the flag, the first thing they’ll see when they fall back is the city gate.”

Fu Jian looked at his son and ordered the banner brought fifty paces forward, with guards still screening it behind the first line of shields. Fu Hong dismounted and went to the banner himself, helping its bearer untangle a rope wound around the pole. Wind suddenly filled the great flag and rocked both man and staff.

The first war horn sounded from Fu Luo’s camp on the north bank. Rebel soldiers raised heavy shields and pressed toward the bridge. The planks were damp and unsuitable for a cavalry charge; armored infantry came forward with a steady thudding of feet. The first man onto the bridge was Fu En, one of Fu Luo’s old retainers. The military officer holding the southern front was Fu Shao. In earlier years both had served under Fu Chong. Fu Shao had once broken through river ice in winter, and Fu En had thrown him the reins that saved his life.

Fu En recognized him at a distance and called him by an old name. Fu Shao’s eyes reddened, but his spear did not move aside. Across the gap came another shout. “Get out of the way! It’s not you I’ve come for!”
“Then whom have you come for?” Fu Shao asked.

Fu En looked toward the Heavenly King’s banner behind the southern line. He was slow to answer. A supervising officer behind him roared a command, and the foremost shields crashed together. The impact numbed Fu Shao’s shoulder. He shouted for his men to lock their shields. He Lanwu pushed up from the side with fresh spears for the front rank. Several young soldiers were shaking so badly they could scarcely grip the shafts. He cursed and drove the weapons hard into their hands.

Arrows came slanting from the north bank, striking the shields and scattering splinters. Qin crossbows answered from the south, and several rebels fell at once. The men behind them could not see who had died and kept pushing forward. The old northern war horns sounded again in the very cadence once used in Fu Chong’s private camps. Two Di soldiers on the southern side shifted their feet before they realized what they were doing. Fu Shao himself nearly turned. He Lanwu lifted a shattered shield and shouted in his face. “Where do you think you’re going?”

Fu Shao clenched his teeth, put his foot back, and shouted to the line to follow the Heavenly King’s flag, not the old horns. A Han crossbowman beside him, hearing the old orders of Fu Shao’s former camp for the first time, hastily loaded a shorter bolt and helped the shieldmen seal a gap. No one in the formation had any strength left to question where the man beside him came from.

The shield wall broke under another violent rush. Two defenders were shoved from the bridge and vanished in the rolling yellow water. Men in the rear stumbled back five paces. The standard-bearer reached out to help a comrade and took an arrow. He fell to his knees in the mud; the flagpole lurched sideways. For an instant the cries from the southern formation became confusion.

Fu Hong ran forward and caught the pole. The river wind struck him almost double. He had never carried a banner so heavy; splinters tore into his palms at once. His guards urged him to return to the central command. He said nothing, merely ordered the fallen standard-bearer carried behind the lines for treatment. Over the noise he called Fu Shao’s name, but his voice was nearly lost.
The banner nevertheless stood upright again.

Fu Shao saw its fabric lift in the wind and felt, for a moment, as though someone had put a hand at his back to hold him steady. He and He Lanwu brought the remaining shieldmen into the breach. Qiang archers loosed arrows just over the spears; one shaft flew so close to Fu Hong’s cheek that it scored a line of blood along his face.
Fu En saw the banner too. He slowed and called toward Fu Shao. “You’ve let the Crown Prince carry the flag?”
“He came of his own accord.”

Fu En looked back at the men behind him. He had believed the Heavenly King was a prisoner in his own palace, that the Qin soldiers were doing no more than serving the men of Yan. Yet the Heavenly King stood beyond the bridge; the Crown Prince carried the banner in the front; even men like Fu Shao, who had served in the old camps, refused to give ground. Fu En suddenly threw down his spear and walked forward with empty hands raised. “I won’t fight!”

The first arrow came from behind and passed through his shoulder. The second buried itself in his back. Fu En pitched forward, half his body sprawled on the bridge planks, one hand still reaching south. Fu Shao roared and tried to vault the shields to help him, but He Lanwu seized his armor straps. The two nearly fell together.
“He can’t be saved now!”
Fu Shao fought him, his eyes bloodshot. He Lanwu held him by the shoulder, his voice rougher than Fu Shao’s. “Do you want the next man shot in the back too?”

The supervising troops on the northern bank loosed another volley. Several of their own men were struck and fell. The rebels' front ranks finally began to disintegrate. Some dropped their swords and crawled across the planks toward the south on their knees. Others dared not surrender and hid beneath the bridge rails. Still others tore the white strips from their standards and fled toward the rear. At first only a few on the south bank cried, “Those who surrender will not be killed!” Then whole ranks took up the call. On hearing it, Murong Chui sent men along the bridge to protect those who laid down their weapons, clearing a path for them to withdraw.

Fu Luo saw what was happening and angrily ordered the drums beaten. Three camps failed to answer. Some were not rebelling against him: they were waiting for a different commander to give the order. Others had brought their families south and dared not close off the only path of escape for strangers. Over ten thousand veterans who had fought hard battles could follow Fu Luo all the way to Chang’an. The other men, gathered hastily along the road, had never shared a single day’s watch beneath the same flag with him. The drummers struck until their arms ached. One white-banded Qin banner after another fell.

Upstream, Beidi horsemen tried three times to ford the shallows. Each attempt was stopped by the barriers Murong Chui had placed and the soil he had ordered broken into soft mud. On the third try two horses bogged down, pitching their armored riders into the shallow water. The mixed cavalry guarding the ford did not ride far in pursuit. They obeyed their orders, held the crossing, and prevented an attack upon the rear.

By late afternoon the last assault from the north had also scattered. Fu Luo had barely two hundred close retainers at his side, though the camp still held many men who had never set foot on the bridge. He could retreat. He might even reach Beidi again and hide behind the gates of the garrisons that feared to open to anyone. His chief secretary begged him, “Your Highness, the northern road is still open.”
Fu Luo looked at the fallen Qin banners on the bridge. “If I go back to Beidi,” he said at last, “who will gather those men’s bodies?”

The secretary had no answer. Fu Luo took off his helmet and handed it to an attendant. He straightened the straps of his armor one last time and ordered the camp gates opened and the bows lowered. Murong Chui came forward to receive the troops. He did not use the word surrender; he merely asked the Duke of Beihai to hand over his sword. He accepted it in both hands and asked, “How many living people still know what happened to Chang Xuan?”
Fu Luo looked at him coldly. “You mean to interrogate me here?”
“I need to know how many living witnesses I must still find.”
The anger gradually left Fu Luo’s eyes. He looked down at the wet ground. “More than you think,” he said at last. “But they may not be willing to speak.”

Fu Luo crossed the bridge in Murong Chui’s custody. Fu En’s body still lay beside the planks. Fu Shao was kneeling over it, covering him with a torn piece of armor, his hands red with blood. Fu Luo stopped to look at the young officer. “Do you still acknowledge the old men of Beidi?”
Fu Shao struggled to answer. “I do.”
“Then how could you bear to hold a spear against him?”
Fu Shao lowered his head. “I never thrust that spear at him.”
“And yet he died.”

Neither spoke across the body. He Lanwu had been binding another wounded soldier’s leg and now came to relieve Fu Shao at his post. “Go and rest for a moment. The surgeons need hands.” Fu Shao remained on his knees until Fu En’s body was lifted onto a stretcher. Only then did he take up his shield and stand.

On the southern bank, Fu Jian had ordered the wounded carried into Chang’an. Two men lay side by side on the first wagon, one Di and one Xianbei. Both cursed the jolting cart through their pain. Fu Hong sat in the surgeons' tent, picking splinters from his palm, a hurried dressing upon the wound on his cheek. He straightened when Fu Luo appeared, but his father asked only, “Will you return to Chang’an and stand trial?”
Fu Luo glanced at the Heavenly King’s banner. Its edge was torn, stained with the blood left by arrows; the standard-bearer had been carried away and no one knew whether he would live.
“Do I still have the right to refuse?”
“You still have the chance to finish what you meant to say while you are alive.”
Fu Luo gave a tired laugh. “If Your Majesty had listened after the spring banquet, would we have come to speak of such things among the dead?”

Fu Jian did not defend himself, nor promise mercy. He ordered Fu Luo confined under the Court of the Imperial Clan. Chang Xuan’s murder, the detention of envoys at East Pass, the fires in Chang’an, and the armed march on Wei Bridge were to be tried separately. Where proof was lacking, rumor alone must not be treated as guilt. Fu Luo looked up as though he wished to say more. In the end he remained silent and went with the guards.

Fu Rong withdrew from East Pass to Anding. When word reached him that the fighting at the bridge had ended, he was still keeping the two contradictory edicts and Chang Xuan’s brief note under guard. He had two other groups of witnesses escorted to Chang’an by separate routes. He had taken no part in the battle at Wei Bridge, but he knew that when it ended, many frontier towns would still be keeping their gates shut against all visitors. His report said: The commander of East Pass is willing to relinquish his troops. Protect the detained officials first. Examine the old registers one by one. Do not be quick to kill because victory has been won.

Near the northern gate of Chang’an, women and children gathered in search of their families. An old woman caught hold of a wagon of prisoners and called out the names of her two sons. The keeper of records searched twice and found the eldest among the captured soldiers; the younger had not been accounted for. The woman clung to the wagon shaft and wept, asking whether the one still living would be allowed home. The guards dared not answer. When the Crown Prince passed, he ordered the lists divided anew into four separate columns: AWAITING VERIFICATION, WOUNDED, DEAD, and NOT RETURNED. No one whose whereabouts were unknown was to be called a fugitive rebel merely because he had not yet been found.

That night the wounded entered the city first, the captives afterward. There were no victory drums for the procession of prisoners, no timber hauled in to build a high platform. Spectators gradually left the roadside. Only the lanterns of those searching for loved ones kept swaying outside the gate. People brought back from the bridge a broken spear, a torn sash, and several wooden name tablets and stacked them in a temporary shelter outside the Secretariat, where they would await those who came to claim them the next day.

Seven days later the military register of merit from Wei Bridge reached the Secretariat. Beside Fu Shao’s name stood: HELD THE BRIDGEHEAD, FILLED THE BREACH, DID NOT RETREAT. Beside He Lanwu’s: SAVED TWO COMRADES. A Qiang archer who had abandoned his assigned place to protect the banner received separate entries for his service and his breach of discipline. Beside the Crown Prince’s own name appeared the words ADVANCED UPON THE BRIDGEHEAD WITHOUT ORDERS. Fu Hong examined the entry and asked his father to record a demerit against him. Fu Jian agreed, but forbade the military law officer to flog the Crown Prince as an ordinary soldier would have been flogged.

Fu Hong’s hand tightened on the edge of the desk. He was not satisfied. Fu Jian told him to preserve the record. “If you have the ability to change this when your time comes, change it so that the rule is fairer than mine.”

North of Wei Bridge, Fu En was finally buried. Fu Shao could not attend the funeral; he was on night watch. When his relief arrived, a Xianbei soldier took his shield and He Lanwu tightened the loosened guard around his forearm. Beneath the camp gate, the keeper of records called the roll. He hesitated when he reached Fu En’s old unit, turned to the new register, and read the next man’s name.
Fu Shao raised his torch and answered.
